summary: Defines a framework for grouping the media lines (m lines) of a Session Description Protocol (SDP) description, using the group and mid attributes. It shows two uses: lip synchronization of audio and video, and receiving one media flow made of several streams on different transport addresses. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 3388.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5888 lets an SDP description label each media line and say which lines belong together. Applications can use those labels to synchronize streams or to describe one media flow that uses different addresses.

subtitle: How SDP names media lines and groups them for synchronized playback or one media flow across several addresses.

tldr.problem: An SDP session can contain multiple media lines, but without grouping information an application cannot tell what relationship the lines have.
tldr.mechanism: A unique mid attribute labels each media line, and a session-level group attribute lists labels under named semantics. This RFC defines LS for synchronized playback and FID for one media flow sent to different transport addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5888 replaces RFC 3388 with an extensible grouping framework and has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

today: RFC 5888 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3388. It has been updated by RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

sections.title: Why Media Lines Need Grouping
sections.content:
A Session Description Protocol (SDP) description can contain multiple media, or m, lines. Without additional information, SDP does not say how those streams relate, so the application receiving the description must decide what to do with them.

RFC 5888 defines a framework using two attributes: mid identifies a media line, and group names a relationship among lines. The framework replaces RFC 3388 and is designed to allow new grouping semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: Several media lines do not automatically say which streams belong together. The mid and group attributes add that missing information to SDP.

sections.title: The mid and group Attributes
sections.content:
Each media line has a unique identification token in an a=mid: attribute. A session-level a=group: attribute gives a semantics token and lists the mid values of the lines in that group.

Every media line in a description that uses grouping must have a mid, including lines not listed in a group. If any line has no mid, applications must not group the media lines. A line with a mid may appear in more than one group, and a group line that names an unknown mid is ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each media line gets a unique name. A group line lists names and says what their relationship means.

sections.title: Lip Synchronization with LS
sections.content:
When media lines are grouped with LS semantics, the receiving application must synchronize their playback. This applies to audio and video, but it can also apply to two streams of the same media type.

For RTP streams, the RFC says synchronization is typically done with RTCP, which lets an application relate timestamps from different streams to local time. The RFC's example groups spoken audio and video while leaving a translated audio stream outside that group.
sections.plainLanguage: LS tells a player to keep grouped streams in step. For example, it can synchronize a speaker's voice with the video of that speaker.

sections.title: One Media Flow with FID
sections.content:
One media instance can use more than one RTP session, for example when different codecs use different ports or when voice and telephone events go to different systems. The RFC calls one media instance, carried by one or more RTP sessions, a media flow.

Media lines grouped with FID semantics form one flow. The sender uses one codec at a time and sends a copy to each grouped line whose codec and direction allow sending. FID must not be used for simultaneous parallel encodings, layered encoding, or lines with the same IP address and port.
sections.plainLanguage: FID lets one media flow have several possible destinations. The sender checks which line matches the codec in use and sends a copy there.

sections.title: Using Grouping in SIP Offers
sections.content:
In SIP offer/answer exchanges, the mid value in an answer must match the corresponding offer, and later offers should reuse that value. Media lines still align by their order in the offer and answer; group and mid do not change that rule.

The offerer requests grouping. An answerer that understands the semantics returns the same group or a subset; one that does not understand it leaves the group out but keeps mid values. A refused media line has port zero and must not remain in a group.
sections.plainLanguage: The offerer proposes how media lines are grouped. The answerer can accept the grouping, return a smaller group, or omit grouping it does not understand.

sections.title: Changes, Security and Registries
sections.content:
RFC 5888 turns grouping into an extensible framework and removes the earlier restriction that a media-line identifier could appear in only one group for a given semantics. It registers the mid and group attributes and a registry for semantics tokens.

An attacker who changes session descriptions could use FID to make a participant send media to an unintended destination. The RFC points to integrity protection for session descriptions and media encryption as mitigations, including S/MIME and TLS for SIP exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: Grouping is now an extensible part of SDP, but altered group information could redirect media. Protecting the session description helps prevent that change.
